comparisons.reference:
Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a fundamental
architecture for graph representation learning through neighbor-
hood aggregation. However, as the number of layers increases,
repeated message passing often leads to unstable representation
evolution, less discriminative node representations, and degraded
performance. Inspired by classical control theory, we introduce a
Proportional-Integral (PI) feedback framework into the propagation
dynamics of GCNs. The proposed method, termed PIGCN, uses pro-
portional feedback to correct layer-wise propagation discrepancies
and integral feedback to aggregate historical correction signals,
thereby stabilizing deep graph propagation, preserving discrimina-
tive node representations, and improving the performance of deep
GCNs. We provide a spectral analysis to theoretically characterize
how PI feedback reshapes propagation dynamics. Comprehensive
experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PIGCN con-
sistently improves multiple representative GCN backbones and
achieves superior performance over representative baselines in
both accuracy and propagation stability. In particular, our PI-Linear
variant achieves 65.15% accuracy on the large-scale Paper-100M
benchmark, demonstrating the scalability and effectiveness of our
framework on large graphs.

However, as the number of layers increases,repeated message passing often leads to unstable representation evolution, less discriminative node representations, and degraded performance. The proposed method, termed PIGCN, uses proportional feedback to correct layer-wise propagation discrepancies and integral feedback to aggregate historical correction signals,thereby stabilizing deep graph propagation, preserving discriminative node representations, and improving the performance of deep GCNs. We provide a spectral analysis to theoretically characterize how PI feedback reshapes propagation dynamics. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PIGCN consistently improves multiple representative GCN backbones and achieves superior performance over representative baselines in both accuracy and propagation stability.In particular, our PI-Linear variant achieves 65.15% accuracy on the large-scale Paper-100M benchmark, demonstrating the scalability and effectiveness of our framework on large graphs.

comparisons.reference:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a standard paradigm
for learning representations from graph-structured data by jointly
exploiting node attributes and graph topology [13, 21]. Through
recursive neighborhood aggregation, GNNs enlarge the receptive
field of each node and capture structural dependencies beyond
local features [13]. This message-passing mechanism has achieved
strong performance on various graph learning tasks, including node
classification, link prediction, and graph-level prediction.
comparisons.ocr: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a standard paradigm for learning representations from graph-structured data by jointly exploiting node attributes and graph topology [13, 21]. Through recursive neighborhood aggregation, GNNs enlarge the receptive field of each node and capture structural dependencies beyond local features [13]. This message-passing mechanism has achieved strong performance on various graph learning tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph-level prediction.

Despite their success, GNNs remain difficult to scale to large
depths. Repeated message passing may make the layer-wise evo-
lution of node representations unstable and progressively less dis-
criminative, leading to degraded trainability and poor general-
ization [3, 27, 32, 43]. As depth increases, graph propagation re-
peatedly mixes neighborhood information and may suppress task-
relevant signals, accumulate propagation bias, and drive hidden
representations toward less informative states. Such depth-induced
degradation can manifest as representation homogenization, low-
dimensional feature collapse, or excessive concentration toward
dominant spectral components [14, 22, 26, 38]. Therefore, regulat-
ing the layer-wise evolution of node representations is crucial for
improving the stability and discriminability of deep GNNs under
repeated message passing.

Repeated message passing may make the layer-wise evolution of node representations unstable and progressively less discriminative, leading to degraded trainability and poor generalization [3, 27, 32, 43]. comparisons.reference:
Existing studies have improved deep graph propagation from sev-
eral perspectives, including residual and identity mappings, normal-
ization and regularization, decoupled propagation, diffusion-based
models, and spectral filtering [1, 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 35, 39, 43]. These
methods alleviate depth-induced degradation by preserving ear-
lier representations, regulating embedding geometry, aggregating
multi-hop signals, or designing frequency-selective filters. However,
most existing methods improve deep propagation by redesigning
the propagation architecture, normalization strategy, or spectral
filter, rather than explicitly controlling how repeated propagation
reshapes spectral components across layers. How to regulate the
spectral evolution of node representations during deep message
passing remains less explored.

However,most existing methods improve deep propagation by redesigning the propagation architecture, normalization strategy, or spectral filter, rather than explicitly controlling how repeated propagation reshapes spectral components across layers. How to regulate the spectral evolution of node representations during deep message passing remains less explored.

comparisons.reference:
Spectral filtering provides an important perspective for under-
standing depth-induced degradation in graph propagation. Re-
peated message passing can progressively concentrate node rep-
resentations toward dominant spectral components, causing non-
dominant components that may carry discriminative information
to decay. Existing spectral GNNs improve this process mainly by
designing or learning frequency-selective filters, such as low-pass,
high-pass, band-pass, or adaptive polynomial filters [1, 6, 9, 16, 18,
20, 39]. However, these methods primarily focus on filter design,
while less attention has been paid to regulating the spectral evo-
lution induced by repeated propagation itself. This motivates us
to study whether feedback-based propagation control can reshape
spectral energy evolution and improve the stability of deep GNNs.
comparisons.ocr: Spectral filtering provides an important perspective for understanding depth-induced degradation in graph propagation. Repeated message passing can progressively concentrate node representations toward dominant spectral components, causing nondominant components that may carry discriminative information to decay. Existing spectral GNNs improve this process mainly by designing or learning frequency-selective filters, such as low-pass,high-pass, band-pass, or adaptive polynomial filters [1, 6, 9, 16, 18,20, 39]. However, these methods primarily focus on filter design,while less attention has been paid to regulating the spectral evolution induced by repeated propagation itself. This motivates us to study whether feedback-based propagation control can reshape spectral energy evolution and improve the stability of deep GNNs.

comparisons.reference:
In this work, we propose PIGCN, a feedback-regulated graph
propagation framework for improving the stability of deep GNNs.
Instead of treating deep graph propagation as a purely feedforward
transformation, PIGCN views it as an iterative dynamical process
and introduces proportional-integral feedback into layer-wise prop-
agation. The proportional term captures the discrepancy between
adjacent propagation states, while the integral term accumulates
historical propagation discrepancies along the depth trajectory.
Through these feedback signals, PIGCN regulates the propagation
dynamics of deep GNNs and reshapes the spectral evolution of node
representations, thereby reducing excessive spectral concentration
and preserving more discriminative information under repeated
message passing. Moreover, PIGCN extends effectively to large-
scale graphs, maintaining competitive predictive performance with
low GPU memory overhead.
comparisons.ocr: In this work, we propose PIGCN, a feedback-regulated graph propagation framework for improving the stability of deep GNNs.Instead of treating deep graph propagation as a purely feedforward transformation, PIGCN views it as an iterative dynamical process and introduces proportional-integral feedback into layer-wise propagation. The proportional term captures the discrepancy between adjacent propagation states, while the integral term accumulates historical propagation discrepancies along the depth trajectory.Through these feedback signals, PIGCN regulates the propagation dynamics of deep GNNs and reshapes the spectral evolution of node representations, thereby reducing excessive spectral concentration and preserving more discriminative information under repeated message passing. Moreover, PIGCN extends effectively to largescale graphs, maintaining competitive predictive performance with low GPU memory overhead.

Another family of methods mitigates over-smoothing through
normalization and regularization [30, 32, 43, 44]. PairNorm pre-
serves pairwise feature distances to prevent node embeddings from
becoming overly similar [43], while DropEdge randomly removes
edges during training to reduce excessive neighborhood mixing [30].
Recent studies further show that residual connections and normal-
ization layers can prevent complete representation collapse, and
GraphNormv2 improves the centering operation to better preserve
useful graph signals [32]. These approaches mainly regulate repre-
sentation geometry, feature scale, or graph connectivity.

Spectral filtering provides another important perspective for
understanding graph propagation. From this viewpoint, message
passing can be interpreted as frequency-selective processing of
graph signals, and depth-induced degradation is closely related to
how repeated propagation reshapes spectral components. Represen-
tative spectral GNNs, such as GPR-GNN, FAGCN, ARMA, BernNet,
DSF, and UniFilter, improve graph learning through adaptive prop-
agation weights, frequency-aware filtering, rational filters, polyno-
mial approximations, or homophily-heterophily adaptive spectral
responses [1, 2, 6, 9, 16, 18, 20, 39]. In parallel, dynamical-system
approaches model graph propagation through diffusion, differential-
equation discretization, or stable graph dynamics [10, 15, 29, 35].
These methods provide useful tools for designing propagation oper-
ators and understanding deep graph dynamics, but they mainly fo-
cus on filter design, propagation formulation, or continuous-depth
modeling.
comparisons.ocr: Spectral filtering provides another important perspective for understanding graph propagation. From this viewpoint, message passing can be interpreted as frequency-selective processing of graph signals, and depth-induced degradation is closely related to how repeated propagation reshapes spectral components. Representative spectral GNNs, such as GPR-GNN, FAGCN, ARMA, BernNet,DSF, and UniFilter, improve graph learning through adaptive propagation weights,frequency-aware filtering, rational filters, polynomial approximations, or homophily-heterophily adaptive spectral responses[1,2, 6, 9,16, 18,20,39].In parallel, dynamical-system approaches model graph propagation through difusion, diferentialequation discretization, or stable graph dynamics [10, 15, 29, 35].These methods provide useful tools for designing propagation operators and understanding deep graph dynamics, but they mainly focus on filter design, propagation formulation, or continuous-depth modeling.

Scaling GNNs to large graphs remains challenging due to the
computational and memory costs of message passing. Existing ap-
proaches improve scalability through sampling, graph partitioning,
sparsification, or coarsening. GraphSAGE uses neighborhood sam-
pling, Cluster-GCN forms mini-batches from graph clusters, and
GraphSAINT samples subgraphs for mini-batch training [5, 17, 41].
Recent methods also explore graph sparsification and coarsening.
SGNN-LS uses Laplacian sparsification to approximate spectral
graph propagation with theoretical guarantees [8], while Graph
Batch Coarsening reduces computational costs through graph de-
composition and coarsening [42]. Although these approaches im-
prove scalability, sampling, sparsification, and coarsening may alter
the effective graph connectivity or introduce approximation errors,
potentially affecting the preservation of structural information.
comparisons.ocr: Scaling GNNs to large graphs remains challenging due to the computational and memory costs of message passing. Existing approaches improve scalability through sampling, graph partitioning,sparsification, or coarsening. Training GNNs on ultra-large graphs is challenging because both
the cost of message passing over edges and the memory required
to store node representations and intermediate activations grow
substantially with graph size and model depth. To address these
constraints, we next show how a light-weigthed PI control leads
to a memory-efficient propagation rule and why it is suitable for
large-scale graph learning.
comparisons.ocr: Training GNNs on ultra-large graphs is challenging because both the cost of message passing over edges and the memory required to store node representations and intermediate activations grow substantially with graph size and model depth. To address these constraints, we next show how a light-weigthed PI control leads to a memory-effi cient propagation rule and why it is suitable for large-scale graph learning.

Evaluation Metrics. We report node classification accuracy as
mean ± standard deviation over random runs, using the check-
point with the highest validation accuracy. To track whether node
representations settle as propagation deepens, we report the Rela-
tive Layer-wise Change (RLC): decreasing values indicate smaller
changes between consecutive layers, and values approaching zero
indicate layer-wise convergence. To assess whether this stabiliza-
tion comes with over-smoothing or loss of representation diversity,
we also report PairSim, Dirichlet Energy, and effective rank. PairSim
tracks node-wise similarity, Dirichlet Energy measures variation
across graph edges (with excessively low values potentially indicat-
ing over-smoothing), and effective rank summarizes feature-space
diversity. Together, these metrics help distinguish stable propaga-
tion that preserves representation differences from stabilization
accompanied by homogenization or feature collapse. Their formal
definitions and interpretations are provided in Appendix B.1.
comparisons.ocr: Evaluation Metrics. We report node classification accuracy as mean ± standard deviation over random runs, using the checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy. To track whether node representations settle as propagation deepens, we report the Relative Layer-wise Change (RLC): decreasing values indicate smaller changes between consecutive layers, and values approaching zero indicate layer-wise convergence. To assess whether this stabilization comes with over-smoothing or loss of representation diversity,we also report PairSim, Dirichlet Energy, and effective rank. PairSim tracks node-wise similarity, Dirichlet Energy measures variation across graph edges (with excessively low values potentially indicating over-smoothing), and effective rank summarizes feature-space diversity. Together, these metrics help distinguish stable propagation that preserves representation differences from stabilization accompanied by homogenization or feature collapse. Their formal definitions and interpretations are provided in Appendix B.1.

To assess the feasibility of PI-based propagation on very large
graphs, we evaluate PI-Linear-8 on Paper-100M and compare it
with MLP, GCN-2, GAT [36], GCNII, GPR/GPR-LS, APPNP/APPNP-
LS, and SGC-3 (Table 3). GCN-2, GAT, GCNII, GPR, and APPNP run
out of GPU memory, while the other methods complete evaluation.
PI-Linear-8 achieves the highest accuracy among the completed
methods (65.15 ± 0.08%), outperforming APPNP-LS (62.10%) by 3.05
percentage points and SGC-3 (62.56 ± 0.13%) by 2.59 percentage
points. These results show that PI-Linear-8 can be applied at the
scale of Paper-100M and achieves stronger accuracy than the listed
baselines that complete evaluation, supporting the feasibility and
effectiveness of PI-based propagation on large graphs.

As shown in Table 4, the full PI model consistently achieves
the best performance across all datasets and backbones. Removing
either feedback term leads to performance degradation, particularly
on heterophilic datasets such as Wisconsin, Chameleon, and Cor-
nell. These results highlight the complementary roles of the two
feedback components: the proportional term corrects current propa-
gation discrepancies, while the integral term accumulates historical
discrepancies to regulate feature propagation. Their combination
enables more effective deep propagation and helps preserve dis-
criminative representations.

comparisons.reference:
We proposed PIGCN, a proportional-integral feedback framework
for stabilizing deep graph propagation. By correcting current prop-
agation discrepancies and accumulating historical discrepancies,
PIGCN regulates the layer-wise evolution of node representations
under repeated message passing. Our analysis shows that PI feed-
back reshapes the effective propagation behavior from a spectral
perspective, helping preserve discriminative information in deep
GNNs. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and representa-
tive backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and compatibility
of PIGCN. Propagation analyses further show that PI feedback
improves deep stability by alleviating representation homogeniza-
tion and maintaining stronger performance at larger depths. On
the large-scale ogbn-papers100M benchmark, PI-Linear-8 achieves
65.15 ± 0.08% accuracy with a peak GPU memory usage of 40.12 GB,
demonstrating the feasibility of PI-based propagation on graphs
with over 100 million nodes. This feedback-regulated view provides
a practical principle for improving the stability and discriminability
of deep graph neural networks.
comparisons.ocr: We proposed PIGCN, a proportional-integral feedback framework for stabilizing deep graph propagation. By correcting current propagation discrepancies and accumulating historical discrepancies,PIGCN regulates the layer-wise evolution of node representations under repeated message passing. Our analysis shows that PI feedback reshapes the effective propagation behavior from a spectral perspective, helping preserve discriminative information in deep GNNs. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and representative backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and compatibility of PIGCN. Propagation analyses further show that PI feedback improves deep stability by alleviating representation homogenization and maintaining stronger performance at larger depths. On the large-scale ogbn-papers100M benchmark, PI-Linear-8 achieves $65.15\pm0.08\%$ accuracy with a peak GPU memory usage of 40.12 GB,demonstrating the feasibility of PI-based propagation on graphs with over 100 million nodes. This feedback-regulated view provides a practical principle forimproving the stability and dicrimiaility of deep graph neural networks.

comparisons.reference:
We compare both the standard GCN and the stronger GCNII back-
bone across depths. Figure 6 compares the classification accuracy
of GCN and GCNII with and without PI control across different
network depths on Cora, CiteSeer, and PubMed. As the network
becomes deeper, GCN+PI generally maintains more stable accuracy
than the vanilla GCN, particularly at 64 and 128 layers, demon-
strating the effectiveness of PI control in mitigating depth-induced
performance degradation. For GCNII, which already incorporates
initial residual connections and identity mapping, the improve-
ments are generally less pronounced.
